content: 1. Exclusive breastfeeding has been shown to significantly reduce the risk of acute respiratory infections and diarrhea-related deaths among infants living in urban slums, such as those in Dhaka, Bangladesh. (Arifeen et al., Pediatrics, 2001) 2. Evidence from Brazil indicates that breastfeeding provides protection against infant deaths caused by infectious diseases. (Victora et al., Lancet, 1987) 3. The mode of feeding plays a critical role in influencing infant mortality and morbidity, with exclusive breastfeeding offering significant protective benefits. (Clavano, J Trop Pediatr, 1982) 4. Exclusive breastfeeding has been demonstrated to have protective efficacy against various health risks in infants. (Kasla et al., Indian J Pediatr, 1995) 5. Breastfeeding reduces the risk of respiratory illnesses in infants, as evidenced by epidemiological studies. (Cushing et al., Am J Epidemiol, 1998) 6. Breastfed female infants have a reduced risk of neonatal respiratory infections compared to their male counterparts. (Sinha et al., Pediatrics, 2003) 7. Breastfeeding lowers both the frequency and duration of acute respiratory infections and diarrhea in infants under six months of age. (Lopez-Alarcon et al., J Nutr, 1997) 8. Topical umbilical cord care at birth, such as the use of chlorhexidine powder, has been associated with fewer cord-related adverse events in neonates compared to dry cord care. (Kapellen et al., Neonatology, 2009) 9. The use of chlorhexidine for umbilical cord care has been shown to reduce neonatal infections and improve outcomes compared to no specific cord care. (Zupan et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2004) 10. Dietary supplementation for lactating adolescent mothers can influence plasma micronutrient levels, which may have implications for maternal and infant health. (Correia-Santos et al., Nutr Hosp, 2011) 11. Postpartum folic acid supplementation in adolescent mothers impacts maternal folate and zinc status, as well as the composition of breast milk. (Keizer et al., Am J Clin Nutr, 1995) 12. Maternal folate status during extended lactation can be improved with supplemental folic acid, which may also affect milk composition. (Mackey & Picciano, Am J Clin Nutr, 1999) 13. Iron and riboflavin supplementation in pregnant and lactating women has been shown to improve hematological parameters in rural populations. (Powers et al., Hum Nutr Clin Nutr, 1985) 14. Postpartum iron supplementation in non-anemic, iron-deficient women improves red cell and iron parameters, as demonstrated in randomized placebo-controlled trials. (Krafft et al., BJOG, 2005) 15. Antibiotic prophylaxis has been shown to reduce postpartum perineal wound complications in randomized controlled trials. (Duggal et al., Obstet Gynecol, 2008) 16. The use of methylergometrine during the early puerperium has been studied in randomized double-blind trials to assess its effects on postpartum recovery. (Andersen et al., Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand, 1998) 17. Maternal and infant health problems following normal childbirth have been evaluated in randomized controlled trials, highlighting the importance of postnatal care. (Ransjo-Arvidson et al., J Epidemiol Community Health, 1998) 18. Antibiotic prophylaxis against postpartum endometritis after vaginal delivery has been compared between amoxicillin-clavulanate and no treatment in randomized trials. (Fernandez et al., Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol, 1993) 19. Prevention of recurrent postpartum depression has been studied in randomized clinical trials, demonstrating the efficacy of targeted interventions. (Wisner et al., J Clin Psychiatry, 2001) 20. Psychological interventions, such as counseling and education, have been shown to reduce the severity of postpartum depression in randomized controlled trials. (Wisner et al., Am J Psychiatry, 2004) 21. Nurse home visiting programs for vulnerable families with newborns have been evaluated in randomized controlled trials, showing benefits for maternal and child health outcomes. (Armstrong et al., J Paediatr Child Health, 1999) 22. Early postnatal check-ups in general practice have been shown to improve maternal health outcomes in randomized trials. (Gunn et al., BJOG, 1998) 23. Community-based postnatal care interventions have been shown to improve maternal health outcomes four months after birth in cluster randomized controlled trials. (MacArthur et al., Lancet, 2002) 24. Peer support programs have been shown to prevent postpartum depression among high-risk women in multisite randomized controlled trials. (Dennis et al., BMJ, 2009) 25. Volunteer home-visiting support programs have been shown to prevent maternal depression during the first year of life in randomized controlled trials. (Barnes et al., Child Care Health Dev, 2009) 26. Exercise and education programs for new mothers have been shown to improve well-being in randomized controlled trials. (Norman et al., Phys Ther, 2010) 27. Massaging babies has been shown to positively affect maternal mood states and reduce salivary cortisol levels in pilot studies. (Fujita et al., Complement Ther Clin Pract, 2006) 28. Exclusive breastfeeding during the first month of life has been shown to reduce neonatal mortality and mortality due to infections in observational studies. (WHO Recommendations on Postnatal Care)
